newsitem.title: USA: Tourists hurt in fierce storm at U.S. space center.
newsitem.headline: Tourists hurt in fierce storm at U.S. space center.

text.p: A fierce storm whipped through NASA's Kennedy Space Centre on Saturday, injuring about 40 tourists and causing minor damage to the launch site, a NASA spokesman said.

Winds gusting up to 52 miles per hour (84 kph) hurled rocks and debris against three double decker tourist buses, shattering windows and showering glass on the occupants, NASA spokesman Joel Wells said. The buses were damaged as they passed close to the space shuttle's 512-foot (156 metre) tall assembly building.

About 40 people, suffering mainly from lacerations caused by flying glass, were treated at a makeshift triage station in the shuttle's launch control centre and at a space centre clinic. Of those, 26 were taken to three local hospitals for further treatment. All were later released.
The freak storm hit the Florida spaceport with little warning shortly before 3 p.m. EST (2000 GMT).
"It was basically a weather assault," Wells said. "One minute it was a nice day, the next, wind, hail, rain and lightning."

Damage to the launch facilities was minor. A mobile office was tossed into a canal, a door on the shuttle assembly building buckled, and bleachers where space centre employees watch launches were left mangled.

The space shuttle Columbia, being prepared for a Thursday blastoff, emerged from the brief storm unscathed. Most of the shuttle orbiter was shielded from the weather by its launch tower, but much of its fuel tank was exposed to the elements.
Public tours, operated for NASA by Delaware North Park Services, were briefly suspended. The visitor centre at the Florida launch site attracts about three million tourists annually.
